title: Lease-based quota reconciliation and proactive load-shedding policy for limiter outages
creator: Aisha Kapoor
description:
Background:
Redwood's quota/limiter layer must be resilient to transient limiter process outages, split-brain lease scenarios, and sudden customer bursts. We have observed two pain modes in production: (1) short-lived limiter process failures causing uncoordinated local fallback that either over-allocates tokens (risking SLO breaches) or drops too aggressively (hurting customer P50 latency due to upstream retries), and (2) burst patterns where static token buckets allow unfair head-of-line bursts for noisy tenants.

Problem statement:
Design and implement a lease-based quota reconciliation protocol plus a proactive load-shedding policy that: (a) preserves global SLOs during limiter outages and inter-region failovers, (b) maintains fairness across tenants under bursty workloads, and (c) minimizes client-visible errors by providing graceful degraded behavior and automatic recovery once the limiter heals.

Goals:
- Introduce short-duration "quota leases" that represent token allocations controlled by a canonical allocator in each region.
- Implement a reconciliation algorithm to resolve overlapping leases after network partitions or process restarts without double-spending tokens.
- Provide a proactive, probabilistic load-shedding policy during degraded states that prefers latency-sensitive tenants and preserves P95/P99 token budgets where possible.
- Back the above with metrics and dashboards, and add automated rollbacks if error budgets are consumed.

Design summary (high level):
1) Lease model: each limiter instance obtains time-bound leases from a regional allocator service. A lease contains: tenant_id, lease_id, token_quota, start_ts, expiry_ts, and a last-ack counter. Leases are sized dynamically based on recent per-tenant QPS and observed burst tail (configurable smoothing window).

2) Escrow and local caching: limiter hot path will use an in-memory escrow counter derived from the lease. When the local limiter node becomes unhealthy or loses connectivity to the allocator, it uses escrowed tokens and switches to a degraded shedding policy when escrow < threshold.

3) Reconciliation protocol: after restart or when reconnecting, limiter instances submit signed lease snapshots to the allocator service which performs deterministic reconciliation: it computes remaining budget by subtracting acknowledged usage (last-ack) and reconciles overlapping leases using a consistent deterministic tie-breaker (lease_id + region_priority). Reconciled deltas are emitted as billing-safe events to the billing queue.

4) Proactive load-shedding: in degraded mode, implement a probabilistic drop policy tuned by three signals: (a) remaining escrow, (b) estimated global token deficit, (c) tenant priority class (latency-sensitive, best-effort). Dropping is randomized per-request with a bias to protect latency-sensitive classes and to smooth bursts across tenants.

5) Circuit breaker integration: router layer observes per-route error and latency signals. If global token deficit persists > 30s and P99 latency exceeds configured SLO delta, the router enables regional circuit-breakers which redirect non-critical traffic to a cheaper model variant or queue-at-client with exponential backoff headers.

Monitoring & SLO mapping:
- New metrics: limiter.lease_acquired, limiter.lease_reconciled, limiter.escrow_remaining_percent, limiter.degraded_drop_rate, limiter.reconnection_gap_seconds.
- Dashboards: serving/runtime/limiter/leases and serving/runtime/limiter/degraded-modes (links below).
- SLOs: correlate degraded_drop_rate with request error SLO (99.9% availability) and latency SLOs (P95, P99). Acceptance if degraded_drop_rate < 0.5% on normal days and system recovers to <0.1% drop within 60s after allocator reconnection during tests.

Testing & rollout plan:
- Unit tests for reconciliation deterministic logic and signed snapshot verification.
- Integration test cluster with simulated network partitions: two-region cluster with allocator failures and restart scenarios.
- Chaos tests: kill limiter processes, inject clock skew, and validate no double-allocations or sustained SLO violations.
- Canary rollout: 1% traffic -> 10% -> 50% with automated guard rails reading degraded_drop_rate and SLO error budget.

Trade-offs considered:
- Lease duration: longer leases reduce allocator load but increase risk of stale double-spend; we choose adaptive leases (1s-30s) based on observed token velocity per tenant.
- Deterministic reconciliation vs. consensus: deterministic reconciliation is simpler and lower-latency; consensus (eg. raft) would be more robust but heavier. We'll revisit if we hit reconciliation edge cases in chaos tests.

Docs & artifacts:
- Design doc: https://confluence.redwood.com/display/SRV/Lease+Based+Limiter+Design
- Prototype PR: https://github.com/redwood/inference/pull/5678
- Load test harness: https://github.com/redwood/inference-loadtests/tree/limiter-leases

Acceptance criteria (concrete):
- No observed double-spend in integration tests across 1M token ops during partitions.
- Canary metrics: degraded_drop_rate <= 0.5% and recovery time <= 60s.
- New metrics populated and dashboard validated in staging.
- Performance: hot-path limiter latency increase < 3us median and < 10us P99.

2026-03-03 - Load test results: Simulated partition for 60s; no double-spend observed in 2M ops. Degraded_drop_rate peaked at 0.9% for 12s and recovered to 0.05% within 42s. Action: tune shedding bias for mid-priority tenants.
